candidates.exact_span: 4Q3             Lowest four-day average flow rate expected to occur once every three-years
candidates.computation_change_reason: Flow-design statistics such as 4Q3 are often used elsewhere to trigger or scale effluent limits and flow-dependent monitoring; a different reading of what 4Q3 denotes (duration, averaging period, or recurrence interval) could change which limits or monitoring conditions are treated as applicable.

candidates.exact_span: BOD             Biochemical oxygen demand (five-day unless noted otherwise)
candidates.computation_change_reason: The parenthetical qualifies whether the five-day BOD form is assumed; interpreting a reported BOD measurement as five-day versus another BOD basis could pair it with the wrong numeric limit or monitoring parameter.

candidates.exact_span: CBOD            Carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (five-day unless noted otherwise)
candidates.computation_change_reason: CBOD is distinguished from BOD in the abbreviations; treating a measurement or requirement as CBOD versus BOD (or versus non-carbonaceous BOD) could change which enforceable limit applies and which monitoring obligation is evaluated.
Critical dilution factors are used in deriving or applying water-quality-based effluent limits; a different interpretation of CD could change the numeric limit used for compliance comparison.
What counts as a DMR shapes whether submitted results satisfy a monitoring obligation and how missing or no-data entries are classified relative to required reporting.

References to ELG elsewhere may invoke federally prescribed numeric limits; interpreting whether a parameter or outfall is ELG-covered changes which enforceable numeric limit is selected for comparison.
ESA-triggered conditions can impose additional or conditional monitoring requirements; whether ESA-based obligations are in scope affects whether monitoring was required for a given period.
Abbreviating fecal coliform as FCB affects mapping reported parameters and permit tables; misidentifying the parameter could apply the wrong numeric limit or monitoring requirement.
Numeric discharge limits are unit-specific; interpreting a limit or measurement in mg/l versus another concentration unit would change whether an exceedance is found.
Confusing ug/l with mg/l (or another unit) when reading limits or measurements would alter numeric compliance comparisons by orders of magnitude.

ML governs how method detection/reporting floors interact with numeric limits and non-detect results; interpreting ML versus other reporting thresholds changes whether a value is comparable to a limit or classified as missing/qualified data.

MQL is distinct from ML in the segment; treating a result as above/below quantification, or substituting MQL for ML, could change compliance comparisons and how no-result or below-quantification evidence is categorized.
O&G is a distinct pollutant parameter; mapping measurements or requirements to O&G versus another grease/oil parameter could change the applicable numeric limit or monitoring obligation.

Reasonable-potential findings often drive whether limits are included and how frequently monitoring is required; a different interpretation of RP could change both selected limits and monitoring applicability.
Settleable solids (SS) is distinguished from total suspended solids (TSS) in the same list; conflating SS with TSS could pair measurements with the wrong numeric limit or monitoring parameter.
pH limits are expressed in standard units; interpreting a pH measurement or limit in non-standard units would change whether an exceedance is determined.
TMDL-based allocations can establish or constrain effluent limits; whether a limit is read as TMDL-derived affects which numeric standard applies for comparison.
TRC is a distinct parameter often subject to seasonal or conditional limits and monitoring; mislabeling chlorine measurements could change applicable limits and whether monitoring was required.
TSS is separately defined from settleable solids; interpreting a solids measurement as TSS versus SS changes which numeric limit and monitoring requirement apply.

WET requirements use non-conventional pass/fail or narrative endpoints rather than ordinary concentration limits; interpreting whether a result is a WET test, how it is reported, or whether data are missing affects limit comparison, monitoring obligation evaluation, and missing-evidence classification.
WLA ties facility-specific pollutant allocations to water-quality-based limits; a different reading of WLA could change the numeric limit selected for compliance review.

BPJ-derived limits may be narrative, conditional, or non-numeric; interpreting a requirement as BPJ-based versus a fixed numeric limit changes whether a compliance comparison is applicable and how absent or qualified results are treated.

Defining BMP as a 'plan' rather than practices could affect whether an obligation is treated as an enforceable numeric limit versus a non-numeric management/monitoring condition, changing both limit applicability and monitoring evaluation.

candidates.exact_span: NMWQS           New Mexico State Standards for Interstate and Intrastate Surface Waters
candidates.computation_change_reason: NMWQS are a primary source for water-quality-based effluent limits; interpreting whether a limit is NMWQS-based changes which numeric standard is used for exceedance determination.
